# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review: "Reduced Working Time at Full Pay" (Halden WP 24-07)

**Arithmetic.** I checked every figure. All the table numbers are internally consistent:
- Organisations sum to 61 and employees to 2,940.
- The employee-weighted output index works out to 98.73.
- Each "per scheduled hour" figure equals the index divided by 0.8.
- Sick days fall 36%, resignations 56%, and 56/61 is 92%.

The problems are in interpretation, not arithmetic.

## 1. The headline productivity gain is largely automatic

"Change in output per scheduled hour" is the output index divided by 0.8. Any organisation reporting output above 80 shows a productivity "gain." So:

- "Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour" is close to guaranteed by the definition. It is not a finding.
- The size of the gain (about 23%) is set almost entirely by the 20% hours cut. It is not evidence of a strong effect.
- The question that matters is whether output was maintained. The answer is mostly yes, but not everywhere: retail and hospitality output fell 6.9%, and healthcare administration fell 3.5%.

The Limitations section says the problems are "unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors." But both the size and the consistency come from the construction of the metric, so neither offers the protection claimed.

## 2. "Sector-general" is contradicted by the paper's own data

This is the most serious problem, because it is the paper's main policy conclusion.

| | Organisations | Reverted | Output index |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail & hospitality | 6 | **3 (50%)** | 93.1 |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | **2 (40%)** | 96.5 |
| All other sectors | 50 | **0 (0%)** | ~99–101 |

- All five reversions came from the two sectors with the weakest output.
- Half of the retail and hospitality organisations abandoned the model.
- The Discussion cites retail's +16.4% as evidence against the view that reduced hours suit only knowledge work. The output data and the revert data point the other way.
- Read honestly, the results look sector-*dependent*: near-full output and universal continuation in office and knowledge work, a material output loss and frequent reversion in coverage-dependent work.
- These sectors also have only 5 and 6 organisations, and the paper gives no confidence intervals. Sector-level claims in either direction are fragile.

Several other conclusions repeat the problem:

- **Summary:** "We conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general."
- **Discussion:** "Even there output per hour rose by 16.4%." This is mechanically true but misleading.
- **Continuation section:** "The high continuation rate is itself evidence." The 92% figure blends the sectors and hides the split above.

## 3. Hours are scheduled, not actual

Limitation 4 concedes that staff who worked their day off, or worked longer on other days, cut their actual hours by less than 20%. The paper then treats this as minor, but it bears directly on the headline:

- If actual hours fell only 10%, the output-per-hour gain is about 10%, not 23%.
- The Discussion and Conclusion drop the word "scheduled" and speak of "output per hour."
- Staggered rosters (17 organisations) and coverage-dependent sectors are where hours were most likely to leak back.

The authors collected actual hours from some organisations. They should report those figures.

## 4. The output measure is the weakest link

- Each organisation's output index is the judgement of a manager responsible for the pilot. That manager signed up to a "100% output" principle and decides whether to continue.
- Each manager used "whatever output records the organisation held." So there is no common metric, and no audit or check against objective data.
- The primary outcome is therefore self-assessment by an interested party. Self-selection, manager reporting and enthusiasm for the pilot all push the same way, so the agreement across organisations is unsurprising.
- Even taken at face value, 98.7 is not 100. The "100% of the output" bargain was missed overall, and labour cost per unit of output rose: about 1.3% across all organisations and about 7.4% in retail and hospitality.

## 5. The revenue figure doesn't show what it claims

- **Inflation.** Revenue is nominal. Inflation in 2023–24 was well above 1.4% in most economies, so real revenue probably *fell*. "No sign that output was sacrificed" doesn't follow.
- **Different baseline.** Revenue is compared with the same months a year earlier. Output is compared with the six months immediately before. The two comparisons can't corroborate each other cleanly.
- **Missing data.** Nine organisations didn't report revenue, and the paper doesn't say which ones. If they were weak performers or the five that reverted, the 1.4% is biased upward.
- **Weighting.** Revenue is weighted by employees rather than by revenue. That needs a justification.

## 6. Attrition and self-selection are understated

- Nine of the 70 enrolled organisations (13%) withdrew before starting, "chiefly for scheduling reasons." In plain terms, they couldn't make the model work. Those are exactly the cases the sector-general claim needs.
- Counting every enrolled organisation (an intention-to-treat basis), continuation was 56/70 = 80%, not 92%.
- The withdrawers would also make a natural, if imperfect, comparison group.
- Manager interviews covered 58 of 61 organisations. The paper doesn't say which three are missing.

## 7. The wellbeing results need more caution

- **Seasonality.** The baseline is the six months before the pilot, which likely includes winter if the pilot started mid-2023. Sick days are strongly seasonal, so the 36% drop may be partly calendar. The paper adjusted revenue for seasonality but not sickness.
- **Resignations.**
  - Employees have an obvious reason not to quit during a trial of a perk they value.
  - Quit rates also fell broadly in 2023 as labour markets cooled.
  - Annualising six months of resignations from small organisations is noisy.
- **Energy fading.** Energy rose 0.61 SD at month three but only 0.29 SD by month six, so more than half the gain had gone. That pattern fits a novelty effect, and the Discussion doesn't mention it.
- **Self-rated productivity.** The 64% who rated their own productivity "higher than before" has no baseline and is highly vulnerable to demand effects.
- **Missing survey details.** The paper gives no survey response rates, and doesn't say whether the same people answered at each wave.

## 8. The causal story is speculative

The Discussion names reduced fatigue as "the most plausible single explanation." The paper's own evidence argues against that ranking:

- Managers described big process changes: fewer meetings (47 of 58 mentioned this), protected focus time, simpler approvals, and less reporting.
- Managers called the shorter week a "forcing device" for changes they had wanted for years.
- The fading energy scores weaken the fatigue account.

The design cannot separate these mechanisms. That matters for policy, because process changes could be made *without* cutting hours. The honest conclusion is that the mechanism is unknown.

## 9. Continuation is weak evidence of productivity

The continuation decision was made by the same self-selected organisations whose managers produced the output index. Reverting also carries a large cost in staff morale once a perk has been given. Continuation shows the arrangement was popular and good for retention. It is not independent confirmation that output held.

## What would make the paper defensible

1. **Retitle the sector claim.** For example: "Output was broadly maintained in office and knowledge-work sectors. Coverage-dependent sectors saw output losses and frequent reversion."
2. **Use output as the primary metric.** Lead with the output index, not the mechanical per-hour figure, and present the per-hour figure only alongside actual hours.
3. **Report the distribution.** Give organisation-level spread (medians, the share below 95, confidence intervals) and outcomes for the organisations that reverted.
4. **Fix the revenue comparison.** Deflate revenue for inflation and state which organisations didn't report it.
5. **Use intention-to-treat figures.** Report all 70 enrolled organisations and use the withdrawers as a partial comparison group.
6. **Adjust for seasonality.** Treat sick days and resignations the same way revenue was treated, or compare with a matched prior period.
7. **Soften the claims.** Drop "unlikely to overturn the main result" and the fatigue-as-main-cause claim.

## Bottom line

The defensible finding is narrower than the one stated. Self-selected, well-prepared, mostly office-based organisations reported near-unchanged output and large improvements in retention and sickness on a 20% shorter schedule. The "+23% productivity" figure is mostly arithmetic. The "sector-general" conclusion runs against the paper's own sector and reversion data.
